This was unveiled in London yesterday and forecasts AI driven consumer spending will hit £370 billion a year globally by the end of the decade.
Carried out in June and July this year in conjunction with Opinium who questioned 13,000 teens and 13,00 parents in pairs across 13 European nations from France and Germany to Italy, Spain, and the UK, the research showed 18% of teens already use an AI assistant, such as ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini, once a week to help them compare products before purchasing. This compares to 9% for the parental adults surveyed.
A third of the surveyed teens said they would happily hand over control to a fully AI run shopping assistant that chooses and pays for products. Speaking at a press event to launch the research, Agnes Woolrich, SVP MasterCard UK, commented: "AI has transformational potential."
"Businesses will have to think differently," she argued, in an exclusive chat with RTIH, who were in attendance at the event prior to the research’s wider general release on 8th September. Woolrich added: "Investments in retailers’ brand, loyalty programmes, and in machine readable digital estates will all be essential in the future, as agentic AI adoption advances."
“I expect the technology to follow the classic adoption curve with early adopters right through to laggards evident. This goes for consumers and merchants," she said, while also unveiling a new artwork commissioned to accompany the report that apes the famous Bayreux Tapestry.
But instead of horses, ships and an arrow in King Harold’s eye as William the Conqueror invaded England from Normandy, the new artwork that Mia Hansson made over three months, shows the story of payments over the last millennium, in the same style as its more famous near namesake.
For example, in 650-490 BCE the first silver coins are embroidered into the new modern Payeux Tapestry artwork, while at the far end there is a panel that shows machine-to-machine (M2M) payments and robotic autonomous commerce, as awaiting us in the future.
“As the Bayreux Tapestry artwork returns to the UK for the first time in almost a thousand years (it’s on display at the British Museum after a loan from its French home), we’ve recreated the story of payments in its inimitable style,” said Woolrich. Other fun embroidered panels in the modern reimagination show the invention and use of contactless cards, digital wallets, and an end-to-end agentic payment, as enacted by medieval looking peasants and nobles.
Futurologists make their predictions
Also at the 7th September launch in London was Magnus Lindkvist (pictured below), one of four futurologists who contributed to the report providing their qualitative predictions for the future, alongside the quantitative ones made by the aforementioned survey.
Speaking exclusively to RTIH, Lindkvist said: “Ultimately, agentic AI commerce is a time saver. It is akin to the washing machine in the huge amounts of time it can save people from doing everyday utilitarian tasks.”
This frees them up for more creative tasks, although Lindkvist did caution that: “The vision of each major technological advancement is never its reality.”
In other words, agentic AI may yet unfold differently, but for now Lindkvist is predicting AI will “get things done” and increase automation on everyday chores in the commerce and transaction chain like subscriptions management. This will allow people to go on more ‘experiential’ physical shopping trips.
“AI is also in a ‘balloon era’, which means it will get reflated even if there is a crash, because it is not in an unjustified bubble,” added Lindkvist.
He thinks the technology is too powerful and useful - on applications in the services layer or on dynamic pricing end uses for instance - to be impeded, even if the stock market does fly too high initially during AI’s early adoption phases. “It’s akin to the dot.com era in that regard.”
The other futurologists involved in the Mastercard sponsored report were: Patrick Dixon; Katja Forbes; and Theodora Lau. Each contributed a chapter to the accompanying book, supported by various Mastercard senior professional’s advice to cardholders, retailers and financial institutions about what to do to be ready for this future.
Dixon looked at shopping and predicted slow websites will lose up to 80% of sales. Enhanced AI enabled search will also turn its results into sales as the agentic element of the technology advances. Plus adoption will be led by the US, UK, China and South Korea, he believes, with new cyber attack risks making some laggard consumers wary.
Forbes focused on retail impacts, such as AI agents networking together to negotiate at scale and therefore get better value for consumers. His future-gazing also foresees AI agents acting as verification tools in future and embedding themselves in wearables like glasses. Wearables will also drive a post-sales data feedback loop.
Lau examined agentic AI’s impact on payments, principally via the end of ‘top of wallet’ thinking and the rise of know your agent rather than customer compliance practices.
Five specific predictions highlighted in the book:
- AI powered shopping becoming mainstream: More than 300 million online shoppers globally could routinely use AI agents to shop and pay by 2030, says the report.
- Routine purchases will increasingly be delegated: Consumers will rely on AI agents for recurring and lower risk purchases in groceries and such-like, thereby saving time and reducing friction.
- Retailers will need to serve both humans and AI agents: Product information, trust signals and digital experiences may become increasingly important as AI agents evaluate products and services. The ability to be machine readable will drive future sale interactions.
- Trust will determine adoption: Security, transparency, accountability and consent are likely to become critical differentiators in an evermore agentic economy.
- Payments will require new identity and authorisation models: Banks, FinTechs and payment providers will need new approaches to authentication, liability and consent as AI agents increasingly participate in modern 21st century commerce.
As AI agents participate in commerce: “Merchants will have to change how they operate,” said Woolrich. “For example, if a consumer buys an airline ticket at present there are clear liabilities and refundability options, during the booking phase. But what about if an agent buys a ticket on behalf of someone? Where's the accountability then?"
"Increasingly menial subscription-based services and automated payments will merge into the agentic AI world to save users time as well," she added, later alluding to how physical and aspirational shopping will become yet more differentiated.
By 2030 the report expects: Payment intent to become as valuable as the payment itself - i.e. consumer authorisation for an agent to purchase will be readable before a purchase is even made; At least three G20 regulators are expected to mandate formal AI agent registration and monitoring by 2030, although the report doesn’t state which three.
Woolrich concluded the event in London by sharing with RTIH that: “The 2030 future envisioned in the report is not that far off”, although she did caution the payments leg of the ecosystem is complex and therefore may be slower to full scale adoption. Those M2M payments may not be emanating from your fridge in an IoT enabled world just yet. But certainly, manufacturing and supply chain reordering is heading that way. The shopping and retail legs are already subject to AI enabled transformation, as detailed in the report. Strap in for the future.
"Mastercard wants to be an enabler in this evolving agentic AI shopping, merchant and payments world - the orchestration layer provider, if you like - that reassures users it is safe, secure, easy, frictionless, connected and worthwhile participating," said Woolrich.
In an accompanying press release, Simon Forbes, President of Mastercard UK & Ireland, had his say on the debate: “For 60 years, Mastercard has been helping people pay and get paid simply and securely. That purpose continues through what could be one of the most significant shifts in decades.”

Tom Scott takes on Technology Manager - Store Projects role at UK grocery retailer Morrisons
Tom Scott is starting a new position as Technology Manager - Store Projects at Morrisons. He has been at the UK grocery retailer for almost five years, and previously helf the role of Technology Product Manager - Online. Scott’s CV also includes a stint at Asda.
NIQ
NIQ and Morrisons have announced a collaboration involving analytics, omnichannel intelligence, and decision-making tools. By leveraging NIQ’s Full View approach, the UK grocery retailer says it is aiming to build “a comprehensive understanding of market dynamics across supermarkets, online grocery, convenience and emerging retail channels, allowing teams to identify growth opportunities and act with clarity and confidence”.
The tie up includes automated reporting capabilities and self-service analytics intended to streamline workflows and support agility across the business.
“Retailers today need the ability to seamlessly turn insight into action,” says Russell Sylvester, NIQ Retail Vertical Lead UK & IRE. “By combining market measurement, consumer intelligence, omnichannel analytics, and advanced capabilities within a single ecosystem, we aim to support Morrisons in building a robust platform for future growth.”
Jen Price, Customer Director at Morrisons, says: “We’re excited to be launching this new collaboration with NIQ, which will deliver product and category intelligence across the full breadth of our retail channels, unlocking value through great insights and helping us make the right decisions quickly, to drive our future growth.”
Everseen
Morrisons is also working with Everseen, deploying its Evercheck solution across 200 of the retailer’s stores in an initial roll-out phase. The platform uses real-time computer vision to simplify the self-checkout process.
The move builds on a trial of the technology. On-screen prompts allow shoppers to correct any missed items themselves, with the aim of keeping queues moving. The software integrates with existing systems, freeing store teams to focus on customer service.
Francesca Bezoari, Store Support Office Director at Morrisons, says: “Our new partnership with Everseen enables us to provide the fast and seamless checkout experience our customers want, while simultaneously equipping our colleagues to maintain the exceptional service that Morrisons is known for.”
Joe White, CEO at Everseen, says: “Morrisons recognise that the best AI solutions deliver measurable results without compromising the customer experience. Our Vision AI platform enables Morrisons to improve its satisfaction scores, proving that operational performance and customer service aren't competing priorities. We're proud to bring our experience from deploying across thousands of global checkouts to support Morrisons transformation.”
So hot right now
Everseen is included in RTIH’s first ever Retail Technology Hot 100 List. Launching in August, this sees us bringing you the hottest companies whose solutions and systems are helping drive the retail sector forward.
Our Founder and Editor, Scott Thompson, drew up a list of 150 companies that had consistently been on his radar over the past 12 months whilst bringing our community the latest retail tech news and views that matter. These companies operate across the omnichannel retail landscape (stores, online, mobile, supply chain, payments etc).
Our judging panel, including Vineta Bajaj, Group CFO, Holland & Barrett, Dan McGrath, JD Group Customer Operations, JD Sports, Dr. Astha Purohit, Director of Product Management, Customer Data and Identity, Walmart, and Paula Bobbett, Chief Data and Digital Officer, Boots, provided feedback on those who have the most innovative, forward thinking technology offerings and are also best addressing retailers' current challenges, painpoints, and opportunities.
The judges used the following framework when making their picks:
1. Retailer problem fit - how meaningful, strategic, and widely felt the retailer pain being addressed is.
2. Production traction in retail (2025–2026) - real named retailer deployments, pilots. 
3. Innovation and defensibility - genuine technical novelty paired with a defensible competitive position.
And there was also a public vote, with thousands of members of our community of retail tech enthusiasts getting involved. Thanks to all those who took part! Based on the judging panel's feedback and the public vote, we then drew up our first ever RTIH Retail Technology Hot 100.
So, without further ado, here are the 100 hottest global retail technology ventures right now. Drum roll, please…

items.title: UK retailers to create 100,000 placements for young people out of work
items.summary: In partnership with DWP, firms such as John Lewis and M&S plan to offer 18- to 24-year-olds placements of two to four weeks UK retailers plan to create up to 100,000 short-term placements for young people not in employment, education or training (Neet) over the next three years to give them a first step on the ladder to paid work. In partnership with the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP), more than 40 retailers, including Marks & Spencer, Pets at Home, Asda and the John Lewis Partnership, will offer Neets aged 18-24 placements of two to four weeks to gain “the skills and confidence needed to take their first step into work”. Continue reading...
items.body:
UK retailers plan to create up to 100,000 short-term placements for young people not in employment, education or training (Neet) over the next three years to give them a first step on the ladder to paid work.
In partnership with the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP), more than 40 retailers, including Marks & Spencer, Pets at Home, Asda and the John Lewis Partnership, will offer Neets aged 18-24 placements of two to four weeks to gain “the skills and confidence needed to take their first step into work”.
The move comes after the former health secretary Alan Milburn warned in a recent report that the 1 million Neets in the UK could rise to 1.25 million over the next five years unless ministers intervened.
Milburn, who is leading a review into Britain’s crisis in youth worklessness, welcomed the retailers’ initiative, saying too many young people were stuck in a vicious cycle of “no experience, no job”, leaving them shut out of employment opportunities.
He said: “Six in 10 young people who are Neet have never had a job. Unless we can increase work opportunities, Britain’s Neet crisis will get worse not better.”
Other employers signed up to the scheme include Tesco, New Look, Wickes, Currys and Greggs.
The prime minister, Andy Burnham, said: “Opportunities like these can make all the difference, helping young people gain the confidence, skills and connections they need to get started in work.”
The scheme, known as Opening Shift, follows the appointment earlier this year of the former M&S chief executive, Marc Bolland, to head a taskforce to tackle the growing youth unemployment crisis.
Bolland, who led the retail chain from 2010 to 2016, has secured the support of retailers for the work placement scheme amid warnings that the country risks a “lost generation” without urgent intervention.
Participants will continue to receive universal credit throughout their placement, mainly because of the logistical barriers claimants face when accepting short-term jobs that mean quitting and then rejoining the welfare programme.
The programme was developed with retailers through the British Retail Consortium and the DWP and has 11,305 placements already pledged.
Bolland, who is also a senior non-executive director at the DWP, is understood to have been chosen for the role thanks to his involvement with the charity Movement to Work, which had already helped more than 200,000 unemployed young people find jobs.
He said: “My work as founder and chairman of Movement to Work showed me first-hand what’s possible when business and government work together to open doors for young people.
“Today’s announcement takes that further, creating thousands more opportunities for young people to build a future in one of Britain’s biggest industries and I’d encourage every retailer to look at what more they can offer.”
Each participant will be guaranteed an interview at the end of their placement, which will vary from 16 to 35 hours each week. Retailers will offer each recruit a “buddy” to help them navigate the new role, with the aim of moving as many recruits as possible into a job should one be available, Bolland added.
The DWP said it would use jobcentres to allow Neets to access the scheme.
Helen Dickinson, the chief executive of the BRC, said: “Retail is uniquely placed to make a difference on the Neets crisis, given the industry’s scale and reach touching every corner of the country.
“Work experience is a first step, and with the right conditions for businesses to invest and create new entry-level jobs, employers across the economy can help tackle the Neet crisis.”

items.body:
Marks & Spencer, Aldi, Lidl and Sainsbury’s among retailers that now hold the Neighbourly Mark
Shoppers and employees can now more easily learn about what sits behind supermarkets’ claims about supporting local communities as part of a new initiative that also shines a light on the charities, food banks and good causes receiving that support. They can do this by clicking or scanning the new Neighbourly Mark, as a number of retailers become eligible to roll it out in stores and online.
Neighbourly is a platform that supports big businesses’ community impact programmes through a network of more than 45,000 vetted local charities and good causes. The Neighbourly Mark is a clickable and scannable participation badge that gives people a direct route to community activity recorded through the venture.
Partners can place the Mark on websites, apps, shop windows and workplace signage as they adopt it. By scanning or clicking on the badge, audiences can access a public Neighbourly profile showing the funding, volunteering and surplus products donated by the organisation through the platform. The Mark also makes community programmes easier for employees to find and recognise, while giving procurement teams a public record of social value delivered.
Steve Butterworth, Chief Executive Officer at Neighbourly, says: “Businesses can say they give back to local communities, but the details are often difficult to find for the people who care about them the most and it is a delicate balance for businesses wanting to publicly evidence their support for good causes. The Neighbourly Mark provides real-time proof in the places people already meet the brand; if you want to know what sits behind the claim, you can simply click or scan it.”
“It is increasingly important to customers deciding who to trust, to employees who want to see what their company contributes, and to buyers looking for evidence of past social value delivery. It also makes the starting point for understanding the company’s commitment much more useful than a claim on its own.”
The founding Neighbourly Mark partners include the following retail, consumer goods, food, drink, and hospitality brands: Marks & Spencer, B&Q, Sainsbury’s, Lidl, Aldi, William Hill, Coca-Cola Europacific Partners (CCEP), Müller, Heineken UK and Pret A Manger.

items.body:
Tillo acquires Amilon and looks to establish dominance in rewards, incentives and gift cards space
Tillo, a rewards, incentives and gift card platform, has announced the acquisition of and a partnership with Amilon, a specialist in digital incentives, gift cards, and employee benefits in Italy. Financial terms of the deal were not disclosed.
Collectively, Tillo and Amilon expect to process over £3 billion worth of gift cards in 2026 and grow 30% year-over-year.
“This is an incredibly exciting landmark moment for Tillo and for our industry. From our very first conversations with the Amilon team, it was clear we shared the same belief in where rewards, incentives and engagement are heading, and the role they play in creating genuine connections between brands, businesses, and consumers,” says Alex Preece, CEO and Co-Founder at Tillo.
“Amilon has built an outstanding business over two decades, trusted by leading Italian and international enterprises and known for exceptional standards of service and expertise. Joining forces gives us the opportunity to combine our strengths and build an international digital value platform with the depth and reach to shape the future of this industry. Equally important, we've found a team whose culture and values strongly align with our own, and I'm proud to welcome them as partners into the Tillo Group.”
"Over the past two decades, Amilon has evolved from a gift card business into a leading digital value platform, helping companies engage, reward and connect with people through an increasingly diverse ecosystem of solutions. This is the next stage in that journey and reflects a shared ambition to help shape the future of digital value, where rewards, incentives, benefits and engagement work seamlessly across markets and channels.”
“By combining Tillo’s global technology and reach with our leadership in Southern Europe and expertise in digital value solutions, incentives and engagement, we are creating a platform with the scale and capabilities to better serve multinational clients, brands and partners. Together, as Tillo Group, we will deliver broader solutions, more advanced technology and new opportunities for growth, while continuing to build on the trusted relationships that have been central to our success,” say Andrea Verri and Fabio Regazzoni, CEOs and Co-Founders at Amilon.
Since 2025, Tillo has been a partner with investor Tenzing as part of a fully secondary transaction that provided liquidity for early investors while enabling the company’s existing leadership team to continue driving its long-term strategy. Beyond its investment, Tenzing has supported Tillo’s next phase of growth by bringing expertise in scaling technology business, expanding internationally and pursuing strategic acquisitions.
"Since backing Tillo, we've been continually impressed by the strength of the leadership team and the pace at which they've scaled the business internationally. The acquisition of Amilon is a natural next step in that growth story, bringing together two founder led, profitable businesses with a shared culture and a complementary footprint across the UK, Europe and beyond. We're proud to continue supporting Alex and the Tillo team, and delighted that Andrea and Fabio are reinvesting alongside us as we build the leading platform for rewards, incentives and gift cards globally,” say Gareth Healy and Maria Tozzi Spadoni, Portfolio Leads at Tenzing.

items.body:
Secret Shopper: Reserved Oxford Street looks the part, but chaotic checkout queues ruin the experience
Reserved’s Oxford Street London street store delivers on fashion, store design and visual technology, but an 18-minute wait to pay and a deeply disappointing checkout experience left Secret Shopper questioning whether this one is worth a return visit.
I had been meaning to go back to Reserved. I had popped into one of its Oxford Street stores previously, spotted quite a few things I liked and made a mental note to return when I had more time. On that first visit I was shopping with my husband, and anyone who has ever attempted a lengthy changing room session while their other half waits nearby will understand why some fashion expeditions are best undertaken alone. If you know, you know.
So, on a recent return to Oxford Street, I went back properly.
There was a sale on, I already had several pieces in mind, and the store was full of clothes I wanted to try. Initially, it was going very well.
Reserved is the flagship fashion brand of Polish retail group LPP and has been around since 1998. It made its UK debut on Oxford Street in 2017 and has since expanded to several locations across London.
In terms of where it sits in the UK fashion landscape, Mango is probably the closest comparison for me. There are bits that remind me of Zara, elements of Uniqlo and COS, although generally at a more accessible price point than the latter, and even touches of the younger Pull&Bear aesthetic.
Most importantly, there are some very, very good clothes.
A store that looks more expensive than it is
Reserved makes a strong first impression. The Oxford Street space is big, contemporary and polished. There is plenty of breathing room between departments, large displays and enormous digital screens running throughout the store.
The checkout area itself is dominated by a huge digital wall, which during my visit was running striking red sale creative across almost the entire space. It looks fantastic.
And that really sums up the first half of the Reserved experience. Visually, the retailer knows exactly what it is doing. The store feels more premium than some of the prices suggest. It is clean, modern and somewhere you actually want to spend time browsing.
And browse I did.
The womenswear range was particularly strong. There were plenty of wearable pieces but enough trend-led stock to make things interesting, and I found myself picking up far more than I had initially planned.
The sizing was also reassuringly predictable. Anyone who shops regularly at Zara will understand why this deserves mentioning. I found Reserved much closer to Mango in terms of sizing, with the clothes generally fitting how I expected them to rather than requiring an existential crisis over whether I had suddenly gone up three dress sizes since breakfast.
The changing room experience was absolutely fine too. There were staff around, clothes were being collected and returned to the shop floor, and the area was being kept organised.
At this point, I was impressed. I had found several pieces I wanted to buy and was already thinking that Reserved could become somewhere I returned to regularly.
Then I went to pay. And this is where everything fell apart.
A huge checkout area and almost nobody serving
The first thing that struck me was the sheer contrast between the size of the checkout operation and the number of people actually working on it. There is a substantial bank of tills underneath that enormous digital wall. Yet when I joined the queue on a busy shopping day on Oxford Street, just two tills were being operated.
And the queue was already long.
I started waiting. And waiting.
One of the two tills was occupied by a customer making an extremely large return. There appeared to be a huge number of items involved, certainly far more than you would encounter during a normal transaction.
That is absolutely the customer's right. If the store accepts the return, the customer is entitled to make it. The problem is that one unusually complicated transaction should not be allowed to bring half of the checkout operation to a halt.
From where I was standing, the items appeared to be being processed individually and the transaction continued for the entirety of my wait.
The customer was still there when I eventually reached a till. That wait lasted 18 minutes (and yes, I did time it!) Eighteen minutes to pay for clothes I had already decided to buy. In modern high street retail, that is an extraordinarily long time.
Oxford Street has moved on, but this checkout has not
What made the situation stranger was where it was happening. Oxford Street is full of retailers that have spent years working out how to remove friction from the checkout.
Uniqlo has its now familiar system where customers place products into a checkout area and the items are recognised without every barcode being individually scanned. Zara has invested heavily in checkout technology. Primark has introduced self-service, as has H&M, while other retailers have simply focused on having enough staffed tills available to prevent queues grinding to a halt.
I do not think self-service is automatically the answer to every retail problem. Far from it.
Who can forget about our awful experience at Pull&Bear, where the technology looked incredibly cool but proved to be a classic case of style over substance. Fancy technology is completely pointless if it makes shopping harder.
At the other end of the scale is M&S, which remains one of my favourite examples of getting self-service right. There are plenty of machines, staff are nearby when customers need help, security tags are dealt with efficiently and the technology generally exists to speed up the experience rather than simply remove people from it.
Reserved had neither. There was no obvious technological solution to absorb the queue, but there also was not enough human capacity to compensate for that.
For a store with giant screens and such a modern visual identity, the actual process of handing over your money felt strangely behind the curve.
The most frustrating part was that nobody seemed concerned
This is where my frustration really started to build. Queues happen. Systems go down. People make huge returns. Somebody arrives at the counter with 25 items. These things are part of running a physical store. The test of good retail is what happens next.
From the queue, I saw what appeared to be a more senior member of staff come out from the changing room area, look towards what was happening at the tills and then return to the changing rooms.
I assumed somebody else would appear. Nobody did. In fact, another member of staff appeared to be taken from the shop floor towards the changing room area while the queue continued to grow.
There were staff elsewhere in the store. During my changing room visit, several people had been working around that area, dealing with clothing, sorting rails and keeping everything organised. All of those jobs matter of course.
But at some point, somebody has to look at a long queue of customers who are literally trying to give the business money and decide that perhaps getting them through the checkout deserves some urgency.
Nobody at the tills appeared to call for additional support. Nobody on the shop floor stepped in. The queue continued moving painfully slowly.
Eventually, after I had been waiting for most of those 18 minutes, a third member of staff arrived at the tills, but by then, the damage was done.
Customer service cannot stop at the changing room door
I do not enjoy criticising individual retail workers. There are countless reasons why somebody may appear disengaged at work, and many of them come back to management, training, staffing levels, workload and whether employees themselves feel properly supported.
That is why I think this goes beyond saying that one particular member of staff should have smiled more. The overall service culture at the checkout felt absent.
When the third till finally opened, the customer ahead of me was called forward. I listened to the interaction and there was no acknowledgement of the queue or thanks for waiting.
When it was eventually my turn, the same happened. No "sorry about the wait". No "thanks for your patience". No "did you find everything you were looking for?"
There was barely any conversation at all beyond what was required to complete the transaction.
After standing in a queue for nearly 20 minutes, that lands badly. A ten-second acknowledgement would not have fixed the operational problem, but it would at least have shown some awareness that the customer experience had fallen well below where it should have been.
Instead, the whole thing felt as though this was simply normal and if it is considered normal, Reserved has a much bigger problem.
Another missed opportunity with the Reserved app
I had plenty of time in the queue, so I did what any retail journalist with 18 unexpected minutes on her hands might do and started investigating the Reserved app.
I downloaded it and discovered that I could get a discount on my first order. Naturally, I was very happy to make use of that. What surprised me was that when I finally reached the checkout, nobody asked whether I had the app, whether I was signed up or whether I wanted to join. I had to raise it myself.
Again, this sounds like a relatively small thing, but it is another part of the experience that did not join up. If you have invested in an app, created incentives to persuade customers to download it and presumably want people using it after they leave the shop, your physical store is surely one of the most obvious places to tell them about it.
Good retail technology is not always about having more technology
There is a bigger retail technology point here, and it is one we keep coming back to in Secret Shopper. The answer is not simply to throw more screens, apps, scanners and self-checkouts into stores. Technology has to solve something.
Reserved already looks technologically impressive. That enormous digital screen behind the tills is impossible to miss. The store has the aesthetic of a retailer that understands modern physical retail.
But customer-facing technology cannot simply be decorative. On this visit, the biggest problem in the store was incredibly basic: customers could not pay quickly enough.
There were numerous till positions, but only a fraction were staffed. A complicated return consumed one of those staffed tills for at least the duration of my wait. There was no alternative checkout route and no visible intervention when the queue built.
That is exactly the sort of friction retail technology should be able to remove. Maybe the answer is self-service. Maybe it is a dedicated returns point so somebody bringing back a huge number of items does not block half the available checkout capacity.
Maybe it is mobile PoS, allowing a member of staff to take straightforward purchases out of the queue. Maybe it is simply a better operational system where an additional till is opened once queues reach a certain length.
There are plenty of possible solutions. Doing nothing should not be one of them.
The frustrating thing is that the clothes are really good
This is what makes the whole experience such a shame. If the clothes had been awful, I would have walked out without giving the store much more thought.
However I really liked Reserved’s offerings. The range is strong. The prices are sensible. The sizing worked for me. The store itself looks excellent. There is a considerable amount here that could make Reserved somewhere I regularly shop.
That is why the checkout matters so much. Retailers sometimes seem to treat payment as the boring functional bit at the end of the customer journey. They fail to remember that it is the final impression.
I had spent a good amount of time browsing, found things I liked, enjoyed trying them on and had reached the point at which Reserved had achieved exactly what every retailer wants. I wanted to spend money! Then the final 18 minutes changed how I felt about the whole visit. By the time I walked out, I was irritated. And that is what I remembered and I am sharing with you now.
There is simply too much competition nearby
This matters even more because Reserved is on Oxford Street. As we have written previously in Secret Shopper, the area has improved dramatically. The days when parts of Oxford Street felt tired and increasingly dominated by shops nobody particularly wanted to visit have given way to a much stronger retail mix.
A customer leaving Reserved has Zara, Mango, Uniqlo, H&M, Primark and countless other fashion options nearby. Move towards Regent Street and Carnaby Street and the competition becomes even stronger.
That means "we sell nice clothes" is not enough. Mango sells nice clothes. Zara sells nice clothes. Uniqlo sells nice clothes. So do dozens of others. The differentiator is the complete experience.
Stores have to make browsing easy, changing rooms pleasant, staff useful and payment painless. If one part breaks badly enough, customers have alternatives a few minutes away. In my case, this visit has made me much less likely to return to Reserved in person.
I may look online because I liked the clothes that much. But after this experience, the idea of going back into the physical store and potentially finding the same queue again is not particularly appealing. That is a serious failure for such an impressive looking store.
Final verdict
Reserved Oxford Street is one of the strangest Secret Shopper experiences I have had because there is so much I should like about it.
The store looks excellent. The clothes are stylish, wearable and fairly priced. The range gives Mango a serious run for its money, and the sizing felt far more predictable than some of its high street competitors. Even the digital presentation is impressive. But retail is not a showroom competition.
The technology has to serve a purpose, staff need the support and training to respond when something goes wrong, and customers should not feel as though nobody has noticed that they have spent nearly 20 minutes waiting to hand over their money.
That is what ultimately ruined this visit for me, too much competition for the final part of the customer journey to be this poor.
I may shop Reserved online again because the clothes impressed me. Would I rush back into this Oxford Street store? After this experience, no. And for a bricks and mortar retailer, that is probably the most damaging verdict I can give.
For the clothes, range and store design, I would give Reserved 4 out of 5. For the checkout experience, queue management and service at the tills, it is 0 out of 5.
Overall, this Secret Shopper experience gets 1.5 out of 5. And even that score is being rescued by how much I liked the clothes.

items.body:
UK retailers team with government as they target 100,000 jobs to tackle youth unemployment crisis
Retailers are joining forces with the UK government with the aim of creating 100,000 jobs for young people not in employment, education or training (NEET) within the current parliament. The tie up comes with a new retail work experience programme to help tackle Britain’s growing youth unemployment crisis, announced at the Retail Jobs Summit in Parliament, alongside DWP Secretary of State, Pat McFadden, Chair of the Young People and Work Review, Alan Milburn, and over 30 retail leaders.
The announcement comes after Milburn’s recent interim Young People and Work Report laid bare the scale of the challenge facing the country. Almost one million, or one in seven young people, are considered NEET. It warns that this could rise to more than 1.25 million over the next five years. Too many are stuck in the vicious cycle of “no experience, no job”, leaving them shut out of employment opportunities, it is argued.
A new work experience programme, Opening Shift, has been developed by retailers through the British Retail Consortium (BRC), and the Department for Work and Pensions with Marc Bolland. Retailers will offer two to four week work experience placements to NEETs aged 18-24, helping them gain the skills and confidence needed to take their first step into work. Participants will continue to receive Universal Credit throughout their placement. Over 40 retailers are involved in the development and roll-out of the new programme with 11,305 placements already pledged.
Every participant will receive an interview at the end of their placement, with the goal of moving as many as possible into a role within the company if one is available. The on the job skills gained through the programme is aimed to support 100,000 NEETs into retail employment by 2029.
The Department for Work and Pensions will build a national pipeline via Jobcentres allowing NEETs to access these work experience opportunities. The work experience will be 16-35 hours each week and provide young people with the necessary skills and experience to then take their first step onto the career ladder with paid employment. Participants will also have a dedicated workplace “Buddy” to support them throughout their placement.
This new programme comes as retailers are also scaling up existing programmes working with DWP under the Youth Guarantee and with partners such as Movement to Work, the King’s Trust and the IGD to build employability skills, work experience and direct hire opportunities for NEETs and provide work experience for those still at school and at risk of becoming NEET.
UK PM Andy Burnham says: “Too many young people are trapped in a vicious cycle where they need experience to get a job and need a job to get experience - leaving them stuck while the world of work drifts further out of reach. That isn't right. It’s great news that retailers across the country are stepping up to offer thousands of young people the chance to get valuable work experience and a route into a job.”
“Opportunities like these can make all the difference, helping young people gain the confidence, skills and connections they need to get started in work. My government is backing British businesses to invest, grow and create jobs, so they can open up more opportunities for young people and build the skilled workforce they need.”
Marc Bolland, Lead Non-Executive Director at DWP, comments: “My work as Founder and Chairman of Movement to Work showed me first-hand what's possible when business and government work together to open doors for young people. Today's announcement takes that further, creating thousands more opportunities for young people to build a future in one of Britain's biggest industries and I'd encourage every retailer to look at what more they can offer.”

items.title: Tesco and Boots lead 100,000 jobs pledge to tackle Neets crisis
items.summary: Tesco, Boots and dozens of other retailers have pledged to create 100,000 new jobs in a bid to tackle the youth unemployment crisis, which they say is trapping young people in a “doom loop”.  A group of top high street firms – which also includes Asda, John Lewis and Marks & Spencer – have joined [...]
items.body:
Tesco and Boots lead 100,000 jobs pledge to tackle Neets crisis
Tesco, Boots and dozens of other retailers have pledged to create 100,000 new jobs in a bid to tackle the youth unemployment crisis, which they say is trapping young people in a “doom loop”.
A group of top high street firms – which also includes Asda, John Lewis and Marks & Spencer – have joined a new scheme to offer young people unpaid work experience, followed by interviews for paid roles.
The commitment to address the youth joblessness crisis comes after a government review found that the welfare state and social media are to blame for this “economic catastrophe”.
Former health secretary Alan Milburn, who led the review, said the number of young people not in employment, education or training (Neet) “will get worse, not better” without more unpaid work experience schemes.
“That is why this new partnership with the retail industry is so welcome. It will give more young people their first foot on the jobs ladder and give employers a bigger pool to recruit from. It is a win-win – and I hope one that other sectors will embrace,” he said.
The group of retailers, represented by the British Retail Consortium (BRC), have worked with the government to develop the programme, which will allow young jobseekers to continue to claim benefits while on work experience.
They will then be given an interview at the end of their placement and given a permanent role if one is available.
Last month, Prime Minister Andy Burnham urged retailers to address the youth unemployment crisis after Sainsbury’s unveiled 10,000 unpaid work experience placements for young people.
Responding to retailers’ commitment to create 100,000 new jobs, Burnham said: “Too many young people are trapped in a vicious cycle where they need experience to get a job and need a job to get experience – leaving them stuck while the world of work drifts further out of reach. That isn’t right.
“Opportunities like these can make all the difference, helping young people gain the confidence, skills and connections they need to get started in work.”
Retailers ‘coming to the rescue’
The retailers will offer two to four weeks of work experience to Neets aged between 18 and 24 and hope to create 100,000 new permanent jobs for graduates of the scheme by 2029. More than 11,000 placements have already been organised, they said.
Tesco will offer 5,000 placements as part of the scheme. Ken Murphy, the supermarket’s chief executive, said: “The retail industry has always been at the heart of local communities, providing jobs that are flexible, secure and accessible.
“The scale of the response from our sector shows retailers recognise the challenge facing the next generation and are determined to be part of the solution.”
Other businesses supporting the commitment include food and drink sellers Greggs, Costa and Pret a Manger, and retailers Amazon, JD Sports and Next.
Earlier this week, John Lewis said that it will prioritise young people when hiring 10,400 seasonal workers over Christmas. “With youth unemployment remaining a significant challenge, we recognise the role we play in providing meaningful opportunities to learn and grow,” chief people officer Helen Webb said.
Helen Dickinson, chief executive of the BRC, said that retailers have “come to the rescue” of Britain’s young people, who are “trapped in a no experience, no job doom loop”.
“Work experience is a first step, and with the right conditions for businesses to invest and create new entry level jobs, employers across the economy can help tackle the NEET crisis,” she said.
Pat McFadden, secretary of state for work and pensions, said: “This partnership will help young people to get the experience employers are looking for. Work experience can be life-changing, giving young people the skills, confidence and connections they need to take their first step into work.”
The commitment comes after the bosses of more than 80 retailers wrote to Burnham in June, urging him to take immediate action to secure the “ladder of opportunity for young people”.
The number of Neets in the UK dipped below 1m in June, but Milburn has warned that this figure could rise above 1.25m over the next five years.

items.title: Retail sales slow as heatwave boost cools
items.summary: The heatwave boost fuelling summer sales cooled last month, as Brits cut back on retail spending to deal with rising bills.  Retail sales grew by 0.7 per cent in the year to August, marking a significant slowdown compared to 3.1 per cent growth in August 2025, according to the British Retail Consortium (BRC).  August’s rate [...]
items.body:
Retail sales slow as heatwave boost cools
The heatwave boost fuelling summer sales cooled last month, as Brits cut back on retail spending to deal with rising bills.
Retail sales grew by 0.7 per cent in the year to August, marking a significant slowdown compared to 3.1 per cent growth in August 2025, according to the British Retail Consortium (BRC).
August’s rate lagged below the 12-month average of 1.6 per cent growth, dragged down by lower spending on big-ticket items like furniture and household appliances.
High temperatures had put a rocket behind retail spending earlier this summer. While the record heat dampened high street footfall, Brits splurged on items like fans and barbecues through online sellers.
But this heatwave boost to consumer spending is cooling as autumn nears, the BRC has found.
Linda Ellett, head of consumer at KPMG – which produced the BRC’s data – said: “Despite temperatures remaining high, summer season cooled off for retail sales in August.”
Record heat caused Brits to kick off their summer spending early, meaning that sales of most categories excluding food and drink are set to run out of steam earlier than expected, she said.
Food sales jumped by 2.6 per cent in August. While lower than the 3.2 per cent 12-month average, this growth dragged up the headline sales figure.
Non-food sales fell by 0.8 per cent year on year in August, compared to the 12-month average of 0.2 per cent.
All eyes on Budget
Harvir Dhillon, lead economist at the BRC, described August as a “disappointing” end to the summer for the UK’s retailers.
“With the cost of household bills rising, and set to rise further, many shoppers have clearly been tightening their belts.
“This was particularly true for discretionary spending, as big-ticket purchases like furniture and household appliances declined and consumers opted to instead treat themselves to smaller luxuries in health and beauty.”
Retailers are ramping up their demands on the government to slash their tax burden ahead of next month’s Budget.
Industry figures have called on Chancellor John Healey to unwind hikes to employer national insurance contributions and reform the business rates system, which they say is blighting the high street with closed-up shops.
“The new government has put high streets at the centre of their vision for better economic growth and the upcoming Budget is an opportunity to deliver on this commitment,” Dhillon said.
“Taking action on business rates and energy costs would help support retail investment in local communities while delivering value for consumers.”

items.title: Next overturns court ruling which forced it to pay shop staff the same as  warehouse workers
items.summary: Shop workers had taken legal action against the fashion chain for paying its retail sales staff lower hourly wages than its warehouse workers.
items.body:
Next overturns court ruling which forced it to pay shop staff the same as warehouse workers
- See more This is Money on Google - save us as a Preferred Source
Next hailed ‘a victory for common sense’ after it won an appeal against a court ruling which forced it to pay shop staff the same as warehouse workers under equal pay rules.
Store workers had taken legal action against the fashion chain for paying its retail sales staff, who are predominantly female, lower hourly wages than its warehouse workers, most of whom are male.
In 2024, a landmark court ruling found that Next was unable to prove that a lower basic wage paid to sales consultants was unrelated to sex discrimination.
But yesterday the Employment Appeal Tribunal ruled that it could pay warehouse staff higher wages than shop workers.
The judgment said this was justified because it costs more to recruit and retain warehouse workers due to higher pay rates in the wider market for these roles.
Next said there was no finding of direct sex discrimination.
Overturned: In 2024, a landmark court ruling found that Next was unable to prove that a lower basic wage paid to sales consultants was unrelated to sex discrimination
The latest development in what has been an eight-year battle will have been monitored by grocers, including Asda, Sainsbury’s and Tesco, which are dealing with similar claims.
Next, which has been run by Lord Wolfson since August 2001, said it believed the judgment ‘is not only correct in law, but also a victory for common sense’.
The retailer added that ‘recruitment and retention pressures’ applying to warehouse workers ‘did not apply to the workforce in its stores’.
Next said that if its appeal had been rejected by the tribunal, ‘it would have created a threat to the ongoing viability of many of our stores’.
The company operates around 458 shops in the UK and Ireland, which employ more than 20,000 workers.
An alternative decision would also have had the ‘perverse effect’ of penalising retailers who operate their own warehouses compared to those who contract out such operations, the retailer said.
A spokesman said: ‘This judgment has come at the right time, the UK economy desperately needs jobs and the loss of this appeal would have represented a hammer blow to retail employment in the UK.’
Elizabeth George, a partner at Leigh Day representing staff, called the latest ruling ‘disappointing’.
She said: ‘The market rate is higher in the predominantly male warehouse labour market, even though the work carried out in stores has already been found to be equal work.’

items.title: Activist investor accuses The Works of unfairly swaying crucial vote
items.summary: The activist investor seeking to tighten its grip on The Works has accused the retailer’s board of attempting to sway a crucial shareholder vote. Kelso, a London-listed activist investor, has been locked in a weeks-long row with the arts and craft retailer, as it attempted to convince shareholders to appoint a former Card Factory executive [...]
items.body:
Activist investor accuses The Works of unfairly swaying crucial vote
The activist investor seeking to tighten its grip on The Works has accused the retailer’s board of attempting to sway a crucial shareholder vote.
Kelso, a London-listed activist investor, has been locked in a weeks-long row with the arts and craft retailer, as it attempted to convince shareholders to appoint a former Card Factory executive to its board.
The Works had sought to slap down the investor’s efforts. It has refused to meet with Graeme Coulthard, the board hopeful, and warned shareholders that his presence on the board would “derail” its strategy.
The Works prevailed when the motion was put to shareholders on Monday, as Coulthard’s board seat was refused by 51.6 per cent of the votes to 48.4.
But John Goold, Kelso’s chief executive, has accused the retailer’s board of inappropriately allowing its Employee Benefit Trust (EBT), which holds four per cent of the company to be issued as bonuses to its management, to determine the vote.
He claims that the EBT – which is run by an independent board of trustees – has voted in line with The Works’ board and slapped down Coulthard’s bid for a board seat.
Kelso: ‘I’m staggered’
Goold told City AM: “In these tight situations, they should not be voting. They definitely should not be deciding who wins.
“Anyone in the City will tell you [EBT] should not be deciding the result of a tight [vote] like this.”
A person close to The Works said that its EBT is administered by an independent trustee company. The board has no control over how it votes in shareholder motions, they said.
Speaking at the group’s Annual General Meeting, Goold praised the retailer’s “standout performance” in recent months, before saying that he was “very disappointed” by its board’s “aggressive reaction” to his push for Coulthard to gain a seat.
What “should have been a day of celebration” had become engulfed by a “really quite needless fallout with a major shareholder”, he said. Goold later told City AM he was “staggered” by the alleged refusal of The Works’ board members to meet with Coulthard.
During its row with the retailer, Kelso has accused chairman Steve Bellamy of switching his primary residence to New Zealand – where he is a citizen – and dialling in to crucial board meetings.
But Bellamy hit back at these claims during the meeting, telling shareholders that Kelso’s accusations are “not correct”. He has remained a dual resident in New Zealand and the UK throughout his chairmanship, he said.
‘Maybe he’s on the bus’
Kelso, which owns 10 per cent of The Works, voted for Bellamy to be ousted as chairman, though he dodged ejection by winning 77.6 per cent of the vote.
The row over boardroom attendance turned on Kelso, when a shareholder questioned why Coulthard had not attended the AGM. “Maybe he’s still on the 212 bus,” Bellamy replied.
Goold told City AM that Coulthard chose not to attend. “There’s no point in having a debate with Graham when he’s there. The board did not speak to Graham ahead of this vote. They just took a view. I’m staggered by it.”
Commenting on Coulthard’s failed bid to gain a board seat, a spokesperson for The Works said: “While 48.39 per cent of votes cast in respect of Resolution 15 were in favour of Mr Coulthard’s appointment, the Board notes that these votes were from a small number of shareholders.
“The Board is grateful for the support of its other shareholders who voted in accordance with its recommendations.”
Ahead of the vote, The Works had warned investors that Coulthard’s presence on the board would “create unnecessary distraction [and] risk derailing” the board’s growth strategy.

items.body:
Shoppers and employees can now find it easier to see what sits behind supermarkets’ claims about supporting local communities, while also shining a light on the charities, food banks and good causes receiving that support. They can do this by clicking or scanning the new Neighbourly Mark, as a host of retailers become eligible to roll it out in stores and online.
Launched by Neighbourly, a giving platform that supports big businesses’ community impact programmes through a network of more than 45,000 vetted local charities and good causes, the Neighbourly Mark is a clickable and scannable participation badge that gives people a direct route to community activity recorded through Neighbourly.
Active partners can place the Mark on websites, apps, shop windows and workplace signage as they adopt it. By scanning or clicking on the badge, audiences can access a public Neighbourly profile showing the funding, volunteering and surplus products donated by the organisation through the platform. This gives greater visibility to the local charities and good causes receiving that support, while giving customers, employees and other audiences clearer evidence of a company’s community impact.
The Mark also makes community programmes easier for employees to find and recognise, while giving procurement teams a public record of social value delivered.
Steve Butterworth, chief executive officer of Neighbourly, said: “Businesses can say they give back to local communities, but the details are often difficult to find for the people who care about them the most and it is a delicate balance for businesses wanting to publicly evidence their support for good causes. The Neighbourly Mark provides real time proof in the places people already meet the brand; if you want to know what sits behind the claim, you can simply click or scan it.
“It is increasingly important to customers deciding who to trust, to employees who want to see what their company contributes, and to buyers looking for evidence of past social value delivery. It also makes the starting point for understanding the company’s commitment much more useful than a claim on its own.”
A corporate partner to a host of major businesses and brands, Neighbourly has delivered over £2.2 billion in social value through its platform since 2014. This included more than £47 million in local grants and funding, 347,000 hours of time-based giving, 358 million meals worth of surplus food redistributed to local charities and good causes, and 6,400 tonnes of product donations.
The founding Neighbourly Mark partners include, amongst others:
- Retail, consumer goods, food, drink, and hospitality brands:Marks & Spencer, B&Q, Sainsbury’s, Lidl, Aldi, William Hill, Coca-Cola Europacific Partners (CCEP), Müller, Heineken UK and Pret A Manger.
- Insurance and financial services providers:TSB, M&G, the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), Arrow Global, Hampshire Trust Bank, Acorn Group, Canada Life UK and Compare the Market.
- Energy, infrastructure, property, and transport organisations:Cadent, Certas Energy, the Transpennine Route Upgrade (TRU), Amentum and Johnson Service Group.
- Technology, professional services, and place-based partners:Hays, Fleet Street Quarter BID and Mills & Reeve.
The founding organisations already use Neighbourly to deliver or record community support through funding, volunteering and surplus product redistribution. They can choose to roll out the Neighbourly Mark online and at locations.
Further organisations interested in partnering with Neighbourly and becoming eligible to display the Mark can find out more at: https://hub.neighbourly.com/for-businesses

items.body:
Accio, Alibaba.com’s agentic AI platform for businesses, today announced it has been appointed as the Official Agentic AI Partner for three premier exhibition organisers: Hyve Group, Business Show Media and Raccoon Media Group. The collaboration will deploy Accio’s ‘Exhibition Agent’ across six flagship European trade shows spanning retail, home & gift, garden, business services, private label and sporting goods.
Accio is Alibaba.com’s agentic AI platform for SMEs and solo founders providing a pre-configured agentic business team that manages the entire SME lifecycle end to end, from market analysis, design and sourcing to store optimisation and inventory monitoring. Globally, more than 10+ million SMEs already use Accio to run their businesses. It requires no code or setup and automates complex tasks such as sourcing, supplier research, procurement and marketing that would otherwise consume hours of manual effort. By embedding this capability directly into official exhibitor directories and floor plans, the Exhibition Agent transforms raw supplier lists into actionable visit plans, ranked matches and post-event procurement workflows, all within a single conversation thread.
This expansion follows the successful pilot of Accio as the Official Agentic AI Partner of Smart Manufacturing Week in June 2026, where the technology supported over 13,000 visitors and 430+ exhibitors at the NEC Birmingham in the UK.
From navigation to negotiation
Unlike traditional trade show apps that offer static maps, the Exhibition Agent acts as an active sourcing partner. Using natural language, buyers can find booths, compare suppliers against their criteria, then hand off to negotiation or logistics agents to draft RFQs and calculate landed costs.
Jackson Szabo, Portfolio Director at Hyve Group said: “Our role as an organiser is to make it as easy as possible for buyers to discover the right products, brands and opportunities, and to make every moment they spend at our shows count. As our events continue to grow in scale and international reach, we need to evolve the way we help visitors navigate that wealth of choice. Partnering with Accio brings a new generation of AI-powered sourcing and planning technology directly into the Autumn Fair, Spring Fair and Glee experience. It will give buyers a more intuitive way to discover relevant exhibitors, plan their time and build smarter routes around the show, while helping our exhibitors become more visible to buyers actively looking for what they offer. We’re excited to be bringing this next-generation technology to our community and to see how it transforms the way people experience our shows.”
“Partnering with Alibaba’s Accio on the Exhibition Agent marks a genuinely new chapter for ISPO in Amsterdam”, said Soraya Gadelrab, Joint MD, ISPO. “Bringing this kind of AI-powered navigation and real-time supplier matching to the show floor is exactly the kind of innovation our exhibitors and buyers need as sourcing gets more complex. We believe this sets a new benchmark for what a modern trade fair experience can look like.”
The solution addresses the cognitive overload faced by buyers at major events. With thousands of SKUs and hundreds of exhibitors, the Agent compresses weeks of pre-event research into minutes, ensuring every booth visit is pre-validated and relevant.
Seamless integration for exhibitors and buyers
The partnership leverages Accio’s newly launched native mobile app. Designed for on-the-go utility, it allows buyers to invoke the Exhibition Agent via voice or image search directly from the show floor.
Key capabilities include:
- Exhibitor-First Sourcing: Searches official directories first, returning ranked matches with booth locations and relevance explanations
- Intelligent Route Planning: Groups matched exhibitors by zone to optimise walking routes and maximise time on the floor
- Visual Sourcing: Allows buyers to upload product photos on the spot to find exact matches among exhibiting suppliers
- End-to-End Workflow: Seamlessly hands off from discovery to negotiation, compliance checks and logistics coordination without leaving the app
- Master Agenda at a Glance: Lets visitors preview all key forums and events ahead of the show, and lock in must-attend sessions so they never miss a key industry insight or networking opportunity
For exhibitors, the integration offers enhanced discoverability, surfacing their profiles to qualified buyers who are actively searching for their specific product categories.The Exhibition Agent is scheduled for full on-site deployment at Hyve Group’s Autumn Fair, Spring Fair and Glee in Birmingham, Business Show Media’s London Business Show and White & Private Label Expo in London, and Raccoon Media Group’s ISPO in Amsterdam.
The Accio app is available for free download on the iOS App Store and Google Play. Attendees of partner trade shows can access the Exhibition Agent features immediately upon registration or via on-site QR codes.

items.title: Record strength El Niño could mean bigger supermarket bills for Australians, experts warn
items.summary: Predicted hot and dry weather in growing areas in eastern Australia identified as ‘one of the key issues’ that will affect food prices over next 12 months Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast The most severe El Niño weather event on record threatens to push food prices higher this year, experts say, piling pressure on households already struggling with the post-pandemic spike in grocery bills and complicating the Reserve Bank’s efforts to bring inflation back under control. The Bureau of Meteorology has forecast El Niño will peak in late spring or summer and “reach levels above the warmest observed since reliable records began in 1950”. Continue reading...
items.body:
The most severe El Niño weather event on record threatens to push food prices higher this year, experts say, piling pressure on households already struggling with the post-pandemic spike in grocery bills and complicating the Reserve Bank’s efforts to bring inflation back under control.
The Bureau of Meteorology has forecast El Niño will peak in late spring or summer and “reach levels above the warmest observed since reliable records began in 1950”.
Michael Harvey, a consumer food analyst at Rabobank research, said the predicted hot and dry weather in key growing areas in eastern Australia was “clearly one of the key issues that will have an impact on food pricing over the next 12 months”.
The Food and Agricultural Organisation in its latest update reported rising weather-related threats are already being reflected in high and climbing global commodity prices.
“It’s a very volatile time, and there are lots of risks around cost re-escalation in the food system,” Harvey said. “There is absolutely risk of food inflation coming through at the consumer end.”
Not all commodities are heading in the same direction, however. For example, dairy and meat prices are beginning to ease after a big recent rise as the underlying fundamentals in those markets shift independently of the looming weather event.
In Australia El Niño created a risk for what is still expected to be a strong winter wheat crop this year, Harvey said.
“That will be the big thing to watch, as well as the spillover effects of that into things like feed grains,” he said, adding that the ultimate impact would be clear by the final quarter of the year.
Even absent hotter and drier weather, overseas shocks have already pushed commodity price benchmarks higher this year, which are linked to local markets through the export trade.
Dennis Voznesenski, CBA’s agricultural economist, said global wheat prices are up by about a third since the start of July, versus about 9% in Australia.
The extreme weather warnings also come as the global oil benchmark, Brent crude, pushed past US$97 a barrel on Monday afternoon to be 35% higher since the start of July.
With diesel prices on the rise again – a key cost for farmers – fertiliser suppliers have also warned of ongoing supply disruptions that will keep prices structurally higher.
Meanwhile, Russia and Ukraine’s record grain harvests are struggling to find their way to international markets after tit-for-tat attacks on critical Black Sea ports.
“A third of global grain exports are stuck right now,” Voznesenski said.
The past five years have seen rapid increases in prices across a range of supermarket goods, contributing to an entrenched cost-of-living crisis across Australia.
In the five years to June, for example, the cost of staples such as breads and cereals, dairy, and other products such as jams and eggs, jumped by between 28% and 30%.
In comparison, in the preceding five-year period to mid-2021, the cumulative increase in these supermarket shelf items was 3-6%, according to analysis of quarterly Australian Bureau of Statistics data.
RBA officials are concerned that a particularly severe El Niño could drive food prices higher and create a further headache later this year, at a time when the central bank is already contemplating whether it needs to raise interest rates again.
But Jonathan Kearns, the chief economist at Challenger, said it was not easy to show a clear link between El Niño events and higher food prices, saying there were a range of costs – from labour to freight and packaging – that often played a bigger role in determining how much Australians pay at the checkout.
“It won’t be a first-order influence on overall inflation, but if you get a little bit extra from food prices, then it’s unhelpful,” Kearns said.
